#1558. Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1. However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs2,3. Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

The global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies. Among these, tidal energy presents a uniquely predictable and substantial resource. Unlike other renewables such as wind and solar, tidal currents are governed by an astronomical cycle, which offers a consistent and forecastable power source4,5. The scale of this resource is significant. Tidal power is estimated at 50 TW h yr−1 in Europe6 and as much as 220 TW h yr−1 in the USA alone7. Near-term deployment targets are 1 GW by 2035 in the UK3, with international roadmaps project deployments eventually exceeding 300 GW worldwide by 20508. These highlight the potential of tidal energy in contributing to energy security and renewable energy portfolios.

Despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an important barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source. A primary challenge is the hydrodynamic load fluctuations that arise from large variations in flow velocity, turbulence, turbine yaw with respect to the incoming stream, velocity shear along the water depth2, wave-induced oscillating currents9, and wake interaction within turbine arrays10. These fluctuating loads are a primary design consideration and are associated with accelerated fatigue, reduced operational lifespans and unplanned downtime. These reliability concerns result in blade and turbine designs with high capital costs, which directly increase the levelized cost of energy (LCOE)3.

To address the challenge of the dynamic loads, various mitigation strategies have been developed. Active control typically deploys systems to actively regulate the pitch11 or camber12 of the blades, therefore, to regulate power output, control mean loads and improve start-up performance. Although the active control systems are effective in certain operational envelopes, the reliability of sophisticated sensors and actuators in the harsh undersea environment remains a concern. Furthermore, the response times of the activator limit effectiveness against rapid, high-frequency load fluctuations13,14.

To address these concerns, there has been an increased focus on developing passive control mechanisms. Passive control is mainly realized in two ways: introducing changes in the blade pitch or modifying the blade camber. Passive pitch control involves designing blades that can rotate around their spanwise axis in response to changing hydrodynamic loads, thereby altering their angle of attack. This is typically achieved by incorporating a pre-loaded torsional spring mechanism at the blade root. Theoretical work in refs. 15,16 are among the first to introduce the concept. Both demonstrated that complete cancellation of the load fluctuation is possible without compromising the mean power. This is followed by a numerical study in ref. 17, which confirmed more than 80% load fluctuations can be reduced in sheared flow conditions, with additional benefits such as faster wake recovery, which improves turbine array performance. Reference 18 has contributed a general framework for the design of passive pitching systems, identifying the locations of the pivot point for maximizing load mitigation. Experimental validations in ref. 19 have confirmed the ability of passive pitching systems in the reduction of time-averaged loadings.

Passive pitching systems are effective for low-frequency, large-scale adjustments and power regulation by adjusting the global angle of attack of the blades. However, the added inertia due to the displacement of the pitching axis required by effective pitching systems, as well as the bearing friction, limits the response of the system to high-frequency disturbances, such as turbulent eddies or rapid shear variations. Moreover, despite being simpler than active control systems, passive pitch blades still introduce extra moving parts and potential failure points in harsh undersea environments. Research has identified that for wind turbine applications, most of the failures originate from the pitch system20, highlighting the significant operational advantage of a robust, passive design.

An alternative design philosophy can be found in nature, where organisms from fish to trees passively reconfigure their shape through distributed material compliance to manage fluid dynamic forces21,22. Drawing from these biological principles, passive morphing flexible blades offer an alternative strategy, where flexibility is distributed along the blade, allowing each blade section to adapt automatically through fluid–structure interaction. Therefore, a faster response time can be achieved with a fixed-pitch blade that does not require hinges and bearings. Passive morphing blades are common in wind energy applications23,24, in which the blade twists to feather in response to a wind gust. This technique, known as aeroelastic tailoring, requires ad hoc structural design, whose scalability and reliability for large tidal turbines is yet to be demonstrated. In fact, for similar power-rated turbines, the bending moment experienced by tidal turbines is higher than that of wind turbines. Therefore, the need for a scalable, reliable, passive system that can mitigate both rapid, localized turbulent fluctuations and slower, large-scale changes in inflow velocity on large-scale tidal turbines remains unmet.

This study directly addresses this challenge by proposing a blade with chordwise flexibility, rather than spanwise flexibility, as in aeroelastic tailoring. The frontal and thickest part of the blade, which provides structural integrity, is rigid. Instead, the trailing edge is flexible from root to tip. Specifically, we provide the first comprehensive experimental demonstration that a carefully designed chordwise-flexible blade can achieve both control of the mean power and thrust with the quasi-steady variations of flow velocities over the tidal cycle (for example, the diurnal tidal cycle) and mitigation of the high-frequency (turbulence) hydrodynamic load fluctuations on tidal turbines, while enabling the same yield as a conventional rigid blade equipped with active pitch control. To demonstrate this potential, we experimentally evaluated the performance of these chordwise-flexible blades against a rigid baseline in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh. The turbine was tested across a range of nominal inflow velocities u∞ = 0.5–1.0 m s−1, and tip-speed ratios (λ) from 3 to 9, with the flexible blades designed for optimal performance at u∞ ≈ 0.85 m s−1. Our analysis first addresses the low-frequency load mitigation over a tidal cycle before examining the high-frequency load fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms of the deformation of the blade. Overall, we demonstrated a new pathway to enhance turbine reliability and survivability, reducing capital costs associated with the active pitch system, and reducing maintenance costs by removing hinges, bearings and actuators, ultimately reducing the LCOE.

The structural design of a tidal turbine is primarily dictated by low-frequency loads, which, in this context, refers to the quasi-steady hydrodynamic loads that change as the mean inflow velocity varies over a tidal cycle. To investigate the potential for load control in this regime, the time-averaged performance of the flexible blades was compared against a rigid baseline. Figure 1 shows the time-averaged power (CP), thrust (CT), and root bending moment (CM) coefficients as a function of tip-speed ratio λ, at all tested inflow velocities. The results demonstrate that the introduction of blade flexibility does not compromise the primary function of energy capture of the turbine. As shown in Fig. 1a, at the rated velocity (uR = 0.878 m s−1) and above, the power coefficient of the flexible blade closely matches that of the rigid blade, achieving a comparable peak CP of approximately 0.37. Notably, the limited value of the maximum CP of both the rigid and flexible blades compared with full-scale state-of-the-art turbines is due to the low Reynolds number at which the model-scale turbines were tested (Methods).

The key advantage of the flexible blade design is its ability to passively regulate peak loadings. At the rated velocity, the thrust coefficient of the flexible blade is comparable to that of the rigid blade near the optimal power-producing tip-speed ratio (λ ≈ 5.5−6), as shown in Fig. 1b. However, the performance of the flexible blades diverges from rigid ones for λ values beyond this optimal range. This high λ region is typically explored by the turbine control strategy to cap power when inflow velocity exceeds the rated velocity. Under these conditions, the flexible blade thrust passively decreases, whereas the rigid one increases. This demonstrates a load-shedding mechanism that can protect the turbine structure during the most demanding high-flow conditions and will be discussed in detail in the next section, in which we simulate the power and thrust a tidal turbine experiences over a tidal cycle. However, at off-design conditions, the flexible blade exhibits higher CT and CM values than at its design speed. While this results in higher thrust coefficients at lower velocities, the absolute forces, which scale with velocity squared (\(F\propto {u}_{\infty }^{2}\)), are much smaller during lower flow periods and are not as important for the structural design of the turbine as the peak loads experienced at or above rated velocity. Therefore, the ability of the flexible blade technology to match power performance while simultaneously offering a passive mechanism to reduce the most important structural loads represents a marked advancement for designing more durable and cost-effective tidal turbines.

a–c, Time-averaged coefficients of power (a), thrust (b) and root bending moment (c) as a function of the tip-speed ratio for rigid and flexible blades at different flow speeds.

To quantify the practical benefits of the passive load mitigation of the chordwise-flexible blade in realistic inflow, we simulate the performance over a representative tidal cycle and compare it against a rigid blade turbine with the same control strategy and a state-of-the-art, actively pitch-controlled turbine (see Supplementary Note 2 for modelling of the active pitch-and-speed control turbine). The sinusoidal inflow velocity represents the flow seen by a tidal turbine during a tidal cycle is shown in Fig. 2a, which is

a–d, Time history over a simulated tidal period of the freestream speed (a), the quasi-steady power (b), the tip-speed ratio (c) and the quasi-steady thrust (d). Data are presented for a rigid-blade turbine with only an active speed controller, a state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed controller, and rubber blades with an active speed controller. All data are divided by the corresponding rated value.

The cut-in velocity of the turbine is selected at u∞/uR = 0.2. The turbine operates at λ = 5.5 when the velocity is lower than rated. At the rated speed, all turbine configurations are operated at the same tip-speed ratio (λR) and provide the same quasi-steady power (PR) and thrust (TR). At higher than rated velocities, λ is such that P/PR = 1. The maximum velocity is set at u∞/uR = 1.2, representative of typical tidal turbine operating conditions.

The simulation first confirms that the passive design of the flexible blade does not compromise its primary function of energy capture. The normalized power profiles shown in Fig. 2b coincide for the rubber blade with speed control and the state-of-the-art active pitch control turbine, where the turbine speed is shown in Fig. 2c. As the total energy harvested is proportional to the integral of the power curves over the tidal cycle, the overlap of the curves confirms a negligible difference in overall energy yield. This demonstrates that the load-mitigation benefits of flexible blades can be achieved without a penalty to energy capture in a real-world setting.

The advantage of the flexible blade design is revealed by the differences in the quasi-steady thrust (Fig. 2d) between the turbine configurations. The state-of-the-art active pitch system limits structural loads by actively feathering the blades into the flow while maintaining the rated rotational speed. For a rigid blade, using only an overspeed-control strategy, the fixed geometry cannot adapt to the increasing flow; solely increasing the tip-speed ratio results in an increasing thrust that peaks at approximately 1.65 times the rated value (Fig. 2c). By contrast, with a comparable speed-control strategy, the passive system of the flexible blade achieves the same quasi-steady power and similar quasi-steady thrust as the active control.

It is also important to note that flexible blades show a slightly higher thrust coefficient at lower, off-design velocities (Fig. 1b) than the baseline rigid blade. However, the absolute thrust force, which scales with velocity squared, is smaller during these periods than the peak values over the tidal cycle. As the maximum loading dictates the primary structural design requirements of a turbine, the nearly identical peak thrust of the passive flexible blade to that of the complex, state-of-the-art active pitch system suggests comparable outcomes for turbine longevity and maintenance costs, representing a marked advancement towards more durable and cost-effective tidal energy systems. Overall, these results indicate that the chordwise-flexible blades can offer a compelling and robust alternative to the state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed control turbine system.

An effective passive system must also address high-frequency load fluctuations, which are a primary driver of fatigue damage. In this context, high frequency refers to the unsteady load components that occur at frequencies of the order of the period of revolution, such as those induced by turbulence, velocity shear or wake interaction, and so on. Figure 3 quantifies the effectiveness of the flexible blades by presenting the standard deviation of load fluctuations relative to the reference rigid blades at rated velocity. To reflect realistic conditions over a tidal cycle, the data for u∞/uR ≤ 1 are presented at the optimal tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5) for maximum power extraction, whereas the data for conditions above the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06) are presented at the higher tip-speed ratio (λ = 8) that is used to cap power. Figure 3 shows a substantial reduction of unsteady loads for all three components when the turbine is operating under its most demanding conditions. At the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.0), where the turbine operates at its optimal λ for maximum power extraction, the flexible blades provide effective fluctuation reduction across power, thrust and root bending moment (mitigated by approximately 18%, 23% and 28%, respectively). Furthermore, even when the inflow velocity increases beyond the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06), the load fluctuation mitigation remains substantial. This demonstrates the powerful and robust damping ability of the flexible blades during both the maximum-power and power-capping phases of operation, when the absolute magnitude of fluctuating forces is greatest. At the lowest velocities (for example, u∞/uR = 0.51), where the blade operates in a stalled condition, fluctuations are known to increase relative to the rigid blade. However, their absolute magnitude is small, reaching only about 15–35% of the fluctuation level of the rigid blade at its rated velocity. A more detailed analysis, presented in Supplementary Note 3, confirms that this mitigation is robust across a wide range of tip-speed ratios under these high-flow conditions.

a–c, Standard deviation of power (a), thrust (b) and root-bending moment (c) of flexible and rigid blades, for the optimum tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5). All quantities are divided by those of the rigid blade at rated velocity.

To illustrate the physics of the passive load regulation mechanism demonstrated previously, the deformation of the flexible blade is visualized at the tip section. Figure 4 shows the phase-averaged digital image correlation (DIC) measurements of the tip of the same flexible blade at a constant azimuthal angle, in which the blade is horizontal with downward velocity. The successful application of this technique using fully submerged cameras represents a significant experimental achievement, as most underwater DIC studies to date have been performed through observation windows rather than submerging the camera in the fluid25. In this way, complex optical distortions and refractive index mismatches associated with viewing ports are avoided, thereby achieving a more accurate measurement. In this study, the DIC system measured the deformation of the suction side of the blade. The full blade profile was then reconstructed by adding the known thickness distribution of the undeformed blade to the measured deformed chord line.

Phase-averaged profiles of one blade tip measured with DIC when the blade span is horizontal, and the tangential velocity is pointing downwards. Coordinates x, y are normalized by the chord length at the blade tip with origin at the quarter chord.

The measurements demonstrate the mechanism of the passive morphing concept. The undeformed flexible blade was designed with a significant initial camber, noticeably higher than that of the conventional rigid blade profile. The high camber present in both the initial blade shape and the subsequent deformed shape before reaching the designed operating point is the primary reason for the higher thrust force generated by the flexible blade operating off-design. Under hydrodynamic loading, the flexible trailing edge deflects upwards, causing the entire profile to flatten into a shape with less camber. This passive feathering becomes more pronounced with higher inflow velocities, which is the mechanism that reduces the thrust coefficient at high tip-speed ratios and velocities.

DIC measurements of different blades (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2) show that blades with lower flexural rigidity undergo greater camber reduction and exhibit stronger load shedding. Specifically, for blades with the same mould geometry, a too-stiff blade results in a too-low pitch and too-high camber, and thus high mean and unsteady thrust. Conversely, a too-soft blade results in an over-pitched blade and low power capture.

The observed mean load-shedding behaviour shown in Fig. 1 arises primarily from quasi-steady passive morphing, and not from dynamic blade deformation resulting in hysteresis, vortex dynamics, and so on. DIC reconstructions of each individual blade at the same azimuthal position reveal only a narrow spread about the mean shape, corresponding to a standard deviation of the pitch variation of approximately ±0.2° (Extended Data Fig. 3).

To further verify that the mean load-shedding behaviour is due to a quasi-steady morphing, we compare the measured blade deformations (Fig. 4) and the corresponding power and thrust (Fig. 1) with those computed with an in-house fluid–structure interaction solver based on a quasi-steady low-order model (Methods). The blade shapes computed with this program are in good agreement with those measured experimentally, and so are the predicted power and thrust for different tip-speed ratios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the numerical solver assumes the blade is in static equilibrium under hydrodynamic loads, these results confirm that the governing physics is quasi-steady.

The fluid–structure interaction of the flexible blades is governed by two non-dimensional groups such as the Reynolds number (Re) and Cauchy number (Ca) (defined in the Methods). The experiments are performed at sufficiently high Re that the hydrodynamic load coefficients are about the same as those at full scale, as shown by the almost identical values for the rigid blade tested at different velocities in Fig. 1. To ensure geometric similarity between the model and the full-scale strain of the flexible blades, the Young modulus E of rubber must be scaled up to maintain the same Ca across scales. As discussed in Supplementary Note 4, rubber features a sufficiently high range of E for full-scale applications. Furthermore, rubber has the advantage of matching the mass density of water, enabling the design of buoyancy-neutral blades and preventing mass-related load fluctuations.

To demonstrate the scalability of the present results, numerical simulations are performed using the in-house fluid–structure interaction solver to model a utility-scale turbine. A rated speed of u∞ = 3.0 m s−1 and a 20-m diameter turbine is selected consistently with modern, state-of-the-art commercial turbines26 and typical energetic tidal sites27. Simulations performed at the respective Re and the same Ca confirm that power and thrust coefficient curves are similar at model and full scale (Extended Data Fig. 5), and therefore the present results are applicable to utility-scale turbines. Although E of the steel spar can be scaled up in numerical simulations, this is not possible in practice. Therefore, different full-scale spar design options are discussed in Supplementary Note 5.

Finally, rubber features high fatigue endurance. Preliminary calculations in Supplementary Note 6 show that the fatigue life of a full-scale rubber blade would substantially surpass the 20 years of service expected by state-of-the-art turbines.

Overall, by allowing similar control on power at thrust above rated speed than active pitch control systems, and mitigating load fluctuations, this technology offers a viable pathway to lower the LCOE. Furthermore, the reduction in load fluctuations enables deployment in energetic, highly turbulent sites previously deemed unviable due to the high fatigue loads. Further analysis of the potential industrial impact of this technology is presented in Supplementary Note 7.

This experimental investigation has evaluated the performance of tidal turbine flexible rubber blades with passive chordwise flexibility, compared against conventional rigid blades. Our results confirmed that the power coefficient of the flexible blade at the design tip-speed ratio is comparable to that of its rigid counterpart, demonstrating that load mitigation benefits are achieved without penalty to the primary function of the turbine as an energy harvester.

The main advantage of the flexible blades is their ability to deform, shedding the excess of load at off-design conditions. This reconfiguration allows control of power by manipulating the angular velocity of the turbine, while achieving passive mitigation of the high-frequency fluctuations that drive fatigue damage.

Therefore, the chordwise-flexible blades offer a compelling and robust alternative to state-of-the-art active pitch control. By mitigating loads with a much simpler setup, the flexible blade eliminates a significant source of potential failure and maintenance costs in offshore renewables.

The mechanism for load mitigation is confirmed through DIC measurement and a quasi-steady low-order code, which shows that the stiffness and initial geometry of the blade produce a controlled ‘feather’ as loads increase. The no-flow geometry and stiffness of the blade are designed so that, under flow conditions approaching the design point, it deforms toward the reference rigid-blade configuration.

Looking ahead, this work opens up new pathways for tidal turbine design and cost reduction. The demonstrated reductions in peak and fatigue loading could allow a reduction in structural requirements for both the blades and their supporting structure, lowering capital costs and enabling higher generator ratings, which in turn improve rated capacity per unit mass. Moreover, the increased robustness from the removal of the pitching system reduces operational and maintenance costs. These factors contribute to a lower LCOE of tidal turbines, addressing the primary barrier to the large-scale deployment of tidal energy farms. By making the technology more financially viable, this technology offers a realistic and attractive option for renewable energy production.

All experiments were conducted in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh, a circular combined wave–current basin designed for scaled testing of offshore renewable energy devices. The tank has a diameter of 25 m and, for the present campaign, was operated in current-only mode with a working water depth of 1.92 m. A schematic of the facility is shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a. The experiments were performed at six inflow velocities in the range u∞ = 0.444–0.923 m s−1, corresponding to a diameter-based Reynolds number,

from 0.49 × 106 to 1.16 × 106, where ν is the kinematic viscosity and d is the turbine diameter. See Supplementary Note 4 for a discussion on the Reynolds number scaling.

FloWave turbulence is between 8% and 9%, and integral length scales of about 25% of the water depth28. These turbulent characteristics are consistent with energetic tidal sites such as, for example, the Fall of Warness29. There, the turbulence intensity is between 5% and 11%, with integral length scales of approximately 30–50% of the channel depth. The mean vertical shear in FloWave is approximately a power law with a 1/12 exponent (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which is only slightly weaker than the 1/10 power-law profile commonly used to represent tidal flows30. Extended Data Table 1 summarizes the comparison between FloWave and the representative tidal sites.

A three-bladed horizontal-axis turbine with a rotor diameter d = 1.26 m was installed in the tank centre, at hub height zhub = 0.876 m. The turbine is equipped with a brushless d.c. motor and a 25:1 planetary gearbox. The main components of the turbine are outlined in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The results presented in the main text refer to four sets of blades: one set of rigid blades used as a baseline and three sets of rubber blades. The baseline rigid blades are CNC-machined (SS316) using a modified NACA 63-415 hydrofoil profile along the span. The profile was modified to ensure a blunt trailing edge, as specified in ref. 31. These blades exhibited negligible flapwise and edgewise deformations. Notably, utility-scale tidal turbine blades exhibit some structural compliance. However, here the model-scale rigid blade was deliberately made rigid to provide a defined geometry.

The main text presents the results for the rigid blades and one set of rubber blades with the optimal stiffness. Conversely, the Extended Data figures also include results for the other two sets of rubber blades, with higher and lower stiffness than optimal. The flexible blades were manufactured by injecting a proprietary rubber mixture into a mould and around a steel spar. All rubber blades have the same mould geometry. See Extended Data Fig. 8 for schematics of the rubber blade. The aeroelastic properties of the blade are tailored along its span by varying the ratio of the rigid spar width to the local chord length, which increases from the tip towards the root with an average of 45%.

The thrust and torque are measured by a force transducer installed between the turbine rotor and the motor shaft (Extended Data Fig. 7). The transducer is bespoke, manufactured by Applied Measurements, rated for an axial load of 1,300 N and a torque of 100 N m, and a resolution of 0.005 N and 0.0004 N m, respectively. In this study, thrust is the net force measured by the hub transducer along the streamwise direction, and torque is the net edgewise moment about the hub axis. Moreover, each blade root was instrumented with a flapwise custom root-bending-moment sensor. Calibration matrices for each sensor were obtained in situ before the test by applying known weights at four points along the cantilever beam attached to the sensor. All force signals were transmitted to a National Instruments NI 9203 acquisition system through a slip ring. The load cells were zeroed without flow before each set of measurements. For each measurement, loads were recorded at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz for 300 s. Rotor angular velocity was measured using an inductive proximity sensor that emitted one pulse per blade pass (three pulses per revolution), enabling determination of the revolution period and computation of the angular velocity.

The principal measured quantities were torque (Q), thrust (T), flapwise root-bending moment (M) and angular velocity (ω). Measured loads and power are non-dimensionalized using standard turbine coefficients:

where ω is the turbine angular velocity in radians per second.

Sensor accuracy and calibration uncertainties were propagated to the non-dimensional coefficients using standard bias-limit uncertainty analysis32, including thrust-torque transducer manufacturer specification (0.1% of full-scale capacity) and primary uncertainties in u∞, ω and geometric parameters. For the present setup, the maximum total bias limits is of order 10−2 for CP and of order 10−2 for CT (representative values). Supplementary Note 1 provides the full derivations and tables.

Blade deformation was measured using phase-locked DIC with underwater cameras and LED illumination (LaVision). The camera system had a fixed focal length of 1.1 m and a field of view of approximately 0.87 m × 0.56 m, sufficient to capture the full blade span (0.56 m). Phase locking was achieved by using the proximity-sensor signal to trigger image acquisition as a blade passed a fixed azimuthal position, with a horizontal span and a downward tangential velocity. For each condition, between 89 and 447 instantaneous deformation fields were recorded over a 300 s period, depending on u∞ and λ.

Images were processed in LaVision DaVis 11 using a subset size of 21 × 21 pixels and a grid step size of 2 × 2 pixels, resulting in a spatial resolution of approximately 0.68 mm near the blade tip (approximately 2% of the tip chord). A reference image in quiescent water was acquired before each set of measurements. In the present configuration, DIC was used to measure the deformation of the suction-side surface of the blade. The full blade profile was reconstructed by combining the measured chord-line deformation with the known undeformed thickness distribution.

A bespoke fluid–structure interaction (FSI) solver was developed for the present study. The solver couples an in-house code based on blade element momentum theory (BEMT), with a panel method with an integral boundary-layer formulation (XFOIL), and a finite element analysis commercial software (Abaqus). The code uses a two-level iterative process, as schematically shown in Extended Data Fig. 9. The process begins with an initial blade geometry. In the outer loop, the BEMT solver is used to calculate the axial and tangential induction factors on a finite number of blade sections at different radial coordinates. Then, the flow velocity and angle of attack experienced by each blade section are computed. These values are used as initial conditions for the inner FSI loop. First, the pressure distributions around each blade section are computed with XFOIL. Then, the pressure distributions from each blade section are combined to obtain a three-dimensional pressure distribution on the blade, which is used as input to Abaqus, in which a new deformed shape is computed. The Abaqus model includes the steel spar. This new shape is then discretized into sections and returned to XFOIL to recalculate the pressure field. This iterative process continues until the blade shape converges. This deformed blade geometry at equilibrium is then fed back into the outer BEMT loop to update the induction factors. This entire two-level process is repeated until convergence. The power and thrust coefficients of the whole turbine are then computed by integrating the loads computed with XFOIL for each blade section and multiplying by three to account for the three-bladed turbine.

This code was used to design the stress-free mould shape for each blade stiffness, ensuring that the equilibrium blade shape matches the reference rigid blade at the design flow speed and tip-speed ratio. The model-scale simulations in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 are initialized with the mould geometry and use the actual stiffness of the metal spar and of the rubber. In the full-scale simulations (Extended Data Fig. 5), the stiffness of both the spar and the rubber is 10.6 times higher than at model scale to ensure that the model and full-scale Cauchy number for both the spar and the rubber is the same, where

where ρ is the fluid mass density and E is the Young’s modulus.

The mould geometry Xi,j is used as input, where i = 0 and j = 0 indicate the iteration number of the inner and outer loop, respectively. The lift and drag coefficient curves (\({C}_{{{\rm{L}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\), \({C}_{{{\rm{D}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\)) are computed with XFOIL for various blade sections, and the induction factors (\({a}_{i,j},{a}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\)) are computed with BEMT. Then the pressure distribution (pi,j(x)) around each blade section is computed with XFOIL and assembled into a three-dimensional load condition for Abaqus, where the new geometry is computed (Xi,j, with i increased by one). The inner loop is repeated till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi−1,j∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵi. If converged, the new geometry is Xi,j, where j is increased by one. The outer loop is repeated from the computation of the lift and drag coefficient for the new geometry, till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi,j−1∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵj.

#1557. Man City survive tunnel clash and Porto fury thanks to Haaland double

Erling Haaland revealed on the eve of this clash how he loves chopping firewood in his spare time – and his goals set alight Manchester City’s Champions League campaign on a fractious evening in Porto.

So much for the new group stage of the competition taking time to warm up. This clash was a hot-blooded, bitter contest that spilt over in the tunnel at half-time, with players getting separated and tempers rising.

And City were not easing themselves back into European action either, they went full throttle at the start of a tough set of group games. With Enzo Maresca, it looks like it will be all-out attack to get the best out of this team.

They can look nervous at the back, particularly with the ball at Gianluigi Donnarumma’s feet, but have attacking weapons to hurt any team in this elite competition. This was a performance that their rivals will take note of.

“It was a complete performance on and off the ball for 95 minutes,” was Maresca’s assessment.

City will certainly scare the traditional heavyweights with Haaland leading their attack and taking an axe to Porto’s defence like he does with logs in his back garden. It was his 58th and 59th goal in 59 games in the Champions League, with his latest an expertly directed header off a post and a calm side-footed finish.

NO MISTAKE from Erling Haaland this time 💪He's put Man City 1-0 up in Porto 🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/UpKOqQA49s

There is an argument that Pep Guardiola could have achieved more in the Champions League, given City’s dominance in domestic football. They have been knocked out by Real Madrid in the last three seasons but this is a new City, different personnel and even a new look.

They wore their black and yellow away kit, inspired by “Manchester’s iconic worker bee” according to Puma, and grafted their way to victory here. Non-stop running going forward, and scrapping with Porto, too.

The Portuguese champions were not happy with Marc Guéhi’s challenge on Gabri Veiga and claimed an elbow was used, with the row carrying on in the tunnel at half-time with security guards separating the players. Rúben Dias also appeared to nudge a Porto official on his way to the dressing room.

“I didn’t see anything but anyway, you can ask how many times you see me or my bench stand up? Zero, for 95 minutes. How many times do you see their bench? So...” Maresca added.

Only Dias and Haaland remain from the starting line-up from the Champions League triumph three years ago, so this is essentially a new team with a new manager.

Erling Haaland seals the deal in Porto 🤝🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/10xSTtZ8nw

Phil Foden, on as a sub in that game, started at Estádio do Dragão after his horse Wreck It Ronnie defeated Najidi Storm, which started the Goodwood race with 1-33 odds and is now the shortest-priced loser in British racing history. The rest of the team are new to City’s challenge.

That includes Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, who was part of a £320m midfield refresh following the departure of Rodri, who was named among the Ballon d’Or nominees a few hours before kick-off to highlight the experience and class City have lost.

Bouaddi, who cost £81.4m from Lille, made a good start in his full debut. The Moroccan teenager is neat on the ball and gets around the pitch, with the next step being able to dominate games like his predecessor.

“In his last game he lost two balls and stayed calm and was back in our box,” Maresca said. “This shows how good he is because any player after two [poor] passes panics, but he is just 18. Erling, Rúben, Mateo [Kovacic], they can manage these kind of games better, but you don’t expect it from a guy of 18. I didn’t see him panic.”

By Bouaddi’s side in midfield was Enzo Fernández, who sought to drive forward into space when City counter-attacked. He was among the players who, along with Dias, were reminded of their Benfica history by the home fans.

Diogo Costa tends to be linked with a move to the Premier League every summer, but has been a one-club man for his career so far. But he showed why clubs are looking at him with his first-half saves to deny Haaland and Rayan Cherki.

Porto’s legendary goalkeeper, Helton, was in the press box at half-time and would have been impressed with the saves, although he was not in his seat when Haaland scored the first goal, which came 94 seconds after the restart.

City had worked the ball around the penalty area, with Antoine Semenyo drawing out Costa before laying off to Fernández. Haaland’s header from the cross had such precision that the goalkeeper did not dive as it angled in off a post.

Still, Porto had their chances with Alberto Costa heading wide from a corner and William Gomes charging down a Donnarumma kick – with City’s most nervous moments coming when they passed around their back line.

Man City are living dangerously here! 🫣Donnarumma nearly gifts Porto an equaliser 😬 pic.twitter.com/otIfZTHmdn

But Haaland sealed the win as the game ticked into stoppage time, finding the bottom corner from Rayan Aït-Nouri’s cutback.

“It was an amazing game against the champions of Portugal. We knew it would be a difficult fight, man against man, they are a top team,” Haaland said. “They play amazing football. All the pressure, we have to deliver on the big stage and that’s what we did. We controlled the whole first half, created chances.”

For Maresca, the victory was also a challenge against Porto’s aggression, with the Italian coach adding: “I was very pleased. We know in this kind of game when you come here it’s always difficult or tricky. The environment, the way they grew up, it’s normal, but I think we dealt with that very good.”

Top performance, Enzo 👊✨ pic.twitter.com/ds0f207tpS

September 13: Manchester United vs Manchester City (Premier League)September 17: Manchester City vs Norwich (League Cup)September 20: Manchester City vs Sunderland (Premier League)October 11: Liverpool vs Manchester City (Premier League)October 14: Manchester City vs PSG (Champions League)

Man City have now won seven of their last eight opening matchdays in the UEFA Champions League 🔵Starting strong 💪 pic.twitter.com/CIjsMj4Dig

“I think we could have scored more goals, especially in the first half. We overall deserved the win and happy with the performance. If you think you can come to a place like this and play and not concede any chances, that is not realistic and it is normal. I am quite lucky as I have a squad of good players. It is a special competition and all the games are very difficult. He [Ayyoub Bouaddi] never panicked and was very good. The performance from him was unbelievable. I am happy to reunite with Enzo [Fernandez], who was very good.”

36 - Erling Haaland scored his 36th UEFA Champions League goal for Manchester City, equalling Sergio Agüero as joint-most for the Citizens in the competition.Inevitability. pic.twitter.com/HHbNadybxh

“I am so happy with how my teammates have welcomed me into the club. They are not just great players but great human beings. The fans have been absolutely brilliant and this is a new step in my career. Erling [Haaland] is an animal, a beast. Every time I am on the pitch, I will look for him and look to assist him. He is an amazing human being and helped me settle in. I am happy Enzo [Maresca] did all he good to make the move happen. I am so grateful for everything he has done for me and my family.”

5️⃣9️⃣ appearances 5️⃣9️⃣ goals@Erling's #UCL record 🤯 pic.twitter.com/v6IvpwC9vm

Tonight: Porto 0 Manchester City 2 (away)October 14: PSG (home)October 20: AEK (home)November 4: RB Leipzig (away)November 24: Napoli (home)December 8: Barcelona (away)January 20: Lens (away)January 27: Sporting (home)

“Amazing game against the champions of Portugal. We knew it was going to be a tough game, they play amazing football. We had to deliver on the biggest stage and we did. We controlled the whole of the first half. We created a lot of chances. They pushed us for a good 25 minutes in the second half but we pulled through. These are the games we have to win. We have had a great start to the season.

“He [Ayyoub Bouaddi] had a really good game and he has been amazing in training. I think we have a gem there. We have to learn and Enzo [Maresca] demands a lot from us. We demand a lot from each other. It was an unreal atmosphere so I hope Enzo is happy with that.”

AEK Athens 1 LASK 0 Club Brugge 2 Aston Villa 3 Dortmund 3 Villarreal 2 Lille 2 Real Betis 3 Porto 0 Manchester City 2 Real Madrid 2 Inter Milan 1

The final whistle is blown and Manchester City begin their Champions League campaign with a 2-0 win in Porto. Erling Haaland’s double gives Enzo Maresca a victory in his first Champions League game in charge of Manchester City.

Enzo has two shots from range in quick succession, one from a free-kick. The free-kick goes just wide and the second is saved by D Costa.

It has been an ill-tempered game and tempers have boiled over again. Rosario and Haaland are involved in a tussle on the floor, which then leads to a mass melee. Haaland and Rosario are both booked for their part in starting that. Haaland is pleased that he got booked but I am not sure why. Both played their part in that melee.

Enzo Maresca’s side will head home with all three points. Ait-Nouri’s cross from the left side of the box picks out Haaland, who first-time shot from 10 yards out picks out the far corner. A clinical finish from Haaland and Manchester City will start their Champions League campaign with a win.

Erling Haaland seals the deal in Porto 🤝🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/10xSTtZ8nw

That is really poor refereeing. Porto are denied two clear fouls before Rosario is then punished for a foul on Enzo, which was a foul but so too were the previous two incidents. Francesco Farioli is then booked for his protestations but you can understand their frustration.

Ait-Nouri has the chance to warp up the three points with an effort from the edge of the box but his shot with his weaker right foot goes narrowly wide.

Nothing comes from the corner as Hwang’s delivery to the front post is dreadful.

Haaland has his fourth headed chance of the game but this one goes over the bar from Ndiaye’s cross. Haaland has scored one of those chances but spurned some good ones.

Down the other end, Fofana, only just on, wins Porto a corner and whips up the home fans.

A final change of the night for Porto sees Fofana replace Veiga. One last roll of the dice from Francisco Farioli.

Whilst Manchester City’s lead is only 1-0, Porto will believe an equaliser is there for them. However, the momentum they were building 10/15 minutes ago has seemingly been lost and the visitors have managed to wrestle back a bit more control.

That is a big chance missed by Pepe. Gimenez receives it down the left and pings a cross to the back post. The cross perfectly picks out Pepe, who fluffs his lines and completely mis-kicks.

Manchester City are making their final two substitutions of the night as Kovacic and Ait-Nouri come on for Bouaddi and Foden. Ait-Nouri looks like he is going to play left wing.

Two more changes for Porto as Silva and M Fernandes are replaced by Gimenez and Moura.

Porto are going to make their first two changes of the night as Hwang and former Norwich man Sainz come on. Varela and Gomes head off.

For the second time in the half, Donnarumma is lucky. To be fair to the Manchester City keeper, the pass back to him is poor but he is then fortunate. His attempted ball out to his left is intercepted by Gomes but it rolls behind for a goal kick. That ball could have rolled straight into the Manchester City net or fallen straight back at Gomes feet with an empty net ahead of him. Donnarumma was very lucky on Saturday against Coventry to avoid a calamitous moment and he is lucky to avoid another awful moment for the second time in quick succession.

Man City are living dangerously here! 🫣Donnarumma nearly gifts Porto an equaliser 😬 pic.twitter.com/otIfZTHmdn

Ndiaye receives it out on the left before driving inside. He gets his shot away from the edge of the box and tries to pick out the far corner but it is too close to D Costa and an easy save for the Porto keeper.

A fine pass from Rosario inside his own half cuts through Manchester City’s midfield sends Varela racing through the Manchester City half. He plays it out to his right to find Gomes, who cuts inside onto his left before trying to beat Donnarumma at his near post but the shot goes wide.

Enzo Maresca responds to a shift in momentum in this game making a double change. Anderson and Ndiaye come on for Cherki and Semenyo.

Porto have started to gain some momentum and they want a penalty. Bouaddi is perhaps a touch fortunate not to be penalised for a foul right on the edge of the box but it may have been just outside the penalty area. You can feel the game starting to turn in Porto’s favour.

Varela is inches away from an equaliser for Porto and plenty of the home fans thought the ball was in the net. Varela sends a curling effort towards goal from the edge of the box but it goes narrowly wide.

That was a glorious chance for Porto to equalise. A corner is sent in from the left to the back post, where Alberto heads it back across goal. However, none of his teammates, including Silva, could tap the ball into the net. Porto should probably be back on level terms.

Donnrumma is a very, very lucky man. Porto would have had a certain penalty as Donnarumma completely flattened Pepe but the latter was offside so it is no penalty. Donnarumma has been booked but avoids a penalty, which would have been a guarantee had Pepe been onside.

Just three minutes into the second half, Enzo Maresca has made a substitution. Gvardiol, on a yellow, is withdrawn and Khusanov is brought on.

Porto’s legendary goalkeeper, Helton, was embracing Daniel Sturridge in the press box and they weren’t in their seats when the goal went in. Lovely move from City and Haaland steered in his 58th goal in the competition.

Erling Haaland moves 7th in the ALL-TIME UCL top-scorers list 💪🇳🇴📊 pic.twitter.com/oIkrPxm0gT

Haaland wasted two headed opportunities in the first half but he does not spurn this chance. It is a first Manchester City assist for Enzo, who clips in a cross from the left side of the box. Haaland meets it and his header glances off the far post and goes in.

NO MISTAKE from Erling Haaland this time 💪He's put Man City 1-0 up in Porto 🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/UpKOqQA49s

Gabriel Clarke on Amazon Prime has reported that there was some trouble in the tunnel as the two sides went off for half-time. Both sets of security teams for the clubs were forced to step in.

We are back under way in Porto. Tempers were really starting to boil over as that first half wore on so will that continue into the second half?

The former Liverpool, Manchester City and Chelsea striker has described the incident involving Marc Guehi and Gabri Veiga as a “nasty collision” and “it does not look good at all”. I think Guehi is a lucky man to still be on the pitch as some VAR officials would surely have recommended a review for that foul. Porto boss Francesco Farioli felt Guehi led with his elbow and the home fans were not happy with that as well as a number of other decisions in that first half.

Marc Guehi absolutely clattered Gabri Veiga 🤯🤕 pic.twitter.com/Fh5ippv3cK

Have your say in the comments section at the bottom of the blog.

Possession: Porto 31%-69% Manchester CityShots: 0-6Shots on target: 0-5Corners: 0-1Touches in opposition box: 0-16

All the stats are massively in Manchester City’s favour but the important statistic, the scoreline, remains level.

The first half is brought to an end and tempers are flaring as the two sides head off, with the game level at 0-0 at the break. The Porto fans and players are not happy with the officiating and Enzo is also involved in some antics.

Gvardiol needs to be careful as he is not punished for delaying a restart when you consider he is already on a booking. The Porto fans want to see a second yellow but the referee says the ball was moving so Porto could not take the restart.

Three added minutes to conclude this first half.

Should Guehi be in trouble here? He appears in real time to win his header but when you watch the replays he led with his arm. He catches Veiga right in the face and Guehi could be in some strife. However, VAR is not going to take any further action and Guehi can count himself lucky. The medics are on to tend to Veiga and you do wonder why VAR has not recommended a review. The ridiculous thing about that was that Guehi was not punished with a yellow card or even a free-kick. That clearly shows the referee did not properly see it.

Porto fans quick to remind Ruben Dias and Enzo Fernandez of their Benfica history. They jeered the pair when they got on the ball. Enzo is getting it from all angles at the moment, with Coventry fans taunting him at the weekend. He can expect more of that in the Premier League after his part in England’s exit at the World Cup, which led to Argentina players holding up a flag saying the Falkland Islands were Argentina’s.

Tensions are boiling over. They have been threatening to do so between Gomes and Gvardiol for a little while and now they do. Gomes steals the ball off Gvardiol and attempts to counter but is pulled back by Gvardiol, who is rightly booked. Gomes is not happy with Gvardiol and they come to blows.

D Costa twice denies Manchester City in a matter of seconds. First he saves from Haaland, then gets to his feet to deny Cherki. Manchester City are knocking on the door and you do feel like a goal is coming for Enzo Maresca’s side.

No goals in Porto but Real Madrid have their second at home against Inter Milan through Fede Valverde.

Manchester City struggled to carve out any genuine chances in the opening quarter of an hour but there are creating more and more opportunities, the latest falling to Foden, whose shot from the right side of the box looking for the far corner is saved by D Costa.

It is not often you see Haaland miss two good chances with his head in quick succession but that is what has happened. Semenyo cuts inside on the left onto his right and curls in a cross into a good area. He picks out Haaland but the Norwegian’s header misses the target. He knows he should have done better as he shakes his head in frustration.

Porto’s front three have struggled to have much of an impact in the game, in particular Silva up top, who has been almost non-existent.

A great save from D Costa to deny Haaland. Foden’s cross just before the byline on the left side of the box picks out Haaland. The Norwegian has barely touched the ball tonight but comes close to opening the scoring. However, D Costa is on hand to deny him with a fine save. Should Haaland have given D Costa the chance to save it? Maybe not.

Diogo Costa CLAWS away Erling Haaland's header 🧤Man City come closest so far in Porto 👀 pic.twitter.com/KVnBHdbNlH

In probably the marquee match-up of the night, Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid are taking on Inter Milan at the Bernabeu. Real have just taken the lead through Kylian Mbappe.

Semenyo cuts inside from the left and gets a shot away from the edge of the box but it is straight at D Costa. That was Manchester City’s first shot of the night.

Veiga has a shot saved at the near post by Donnarumma but the offside flag goes up. Veiga and Pep exchange a neat one-two down Porto’s left before Veiga’s effort is saved but Pepe was offside in the build-up.

Manchester City are dominating possession and perhaps it was a ploy by Enzo Marecsa to take it slowly and hog the ball in order to take the early sting out of Porto. The visitors would have been expecting the hosts would want to start hot so maybe they were willing to be slow on the ball in order to quieten down the crowd early doors. They have not had a shot yet and not really threatened the Porto goal but the hosts have not offered much going forward.

The weather in Porto really is horrible, the type of weather you would expect in Manchester in mid-November than Porto in early September.

Porto have a strong defensive record thus far this season but undoubtedly they will be tested a lot more tonight than they are in Liga Portugal. You would also imagine they will have to be clinical in attack as they are unlikely to create as many chances as they do domestically.

With it hammering down, Porto boss Francesco Farioli has swapped his lovely suit that he was wearing pre-game for a tracksuit top and cap. At half-time, he will probably head back in drenched like all the players if he is active in his dugout.

We are under way at the Estádio do Dragão with the rain still teaming down in Porto. Manchester City’s Champions League campaign gets going.

It has been pouring down in Porto but that has not dampened the spirits of the home fans, who are in fine voice ahead of kick-off. The pyrotechnics have gone off and it is loud inside the Dragão. Both sides then emerge from the tunnel and here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Porto: Diogo Costa; Varela, Perez, Kiwior, Alberto Costa; Rosario, Martim Fernandes, Veiga; Gomes, Silva, Pepe.Substitutes: Claudio Ramos, Joao Costa, Hwang, Sainz, Gimenez, Souza, Fofana, Cunha, Silva, L.Gomes, Moura.

Manchester City: Donnarumma; Nunes, Dias, Guehi Gvardiol; Bouaddi, Fernandez, Cherki; Foden, Haaland, Semenyo.Substitutes: Bettinelli, Rulli, Anderson, Ndiaye, Kovacic, Ait-Nouri, Reis, Allan, Khusanov, McAidoo, Lewis.

It has been a decent day for Phil Foden already. The City forward’s race horse, Wreck It Ronnie, won at Goodwood and set a new record in the sport. The horse named after his son defeated Najidi Storm, which was started the race with 1-33 odds. It means the favourite is now the shortest-priced loser in British racing history. Foden’s family also call him “Ronnie”, which is the name he gave his son.

Will Enzo Fernández live up to the price tag for Man City? 💰@DanielSturridge tells us what he thinks he'll add to Maresca's men 💪 pic.twitter.com/ZLKdrFeTmV

The referee tonight in Porto is Szymon Marciniak, which may not be a good omen considering Manchester City have been knocked out of the Champions League in the last three seasons. The Polish referee was branded a “Madridista” last year after being pictured with a Real wash bag in the dressing room. Barcelona were unhappy with this after he took charge of a clash against Inter Milan which ended in an epic defeat.

Aston Villa have held on to beat Club Brugge 3-2 and you can catch all the reaction to that game right here.

The big news here at Estádio do Dragão is that Ayyoub Bouaddi is given his full Manchester City debut, after coming off the bench in previous Premier League games. The Morocco midfielder, 18, starts in midfield in place of Elliot Anderson from the team that defeated Coventry at the weekend. Phil Foden is also given the nod, replacing Iliman Ndiaye.

The Opta Supercomputer, before a ball was kicked tonight, has produced these numbers for what it thinks about who might win the Champions League this season:

57 - Of Erling Haaland's 300 top-flight club goals, 57 have come in the UEFA Champions League, more than any other player since his debut in the competition in September 2019.Continental. pic.twitter.com/lJdzuCwjEf

Are you ready? WE ARE 💙 pic.twitter.com/SoIuejqFIV

The Argentine started for Manchester City on Saturday against Coventry and he once more takes a place in the centre of their midfield tonight. He starts alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi to form a £200m+ starting midfield pairing.

Aston Villa are into the second half of their game over at Club Brugge. As they kicked off in the second half, Villa were 3-1 up but Brugge have got a goal back. It could be a nervy finish for Unai Emery’s side and you can follow the conclusion of that match right here.

In the forward line for Porto tonight is Brazilian winger William Gomes. The 20-year-old joined Porto from Sao Paulo in 2025 and already has four goal involvements (two goals, two assists) to his name in Liga Portugal this season. He was linked with a move to the Premier League over the summer and you would expect will continue to be on the radar of English clubs going forward.

It has been a positive start for Unai Emery’s Aston Villa out in Belgium as they lead Club Brugge 3-1 at half-time.

Enzo Maresca takes charge of his first Champions League game in charge of Manchester City as they have travelled to Portugal to take on Porto at the Estadio do Dragao. These sides last met during the Champions League group stages during the 2020/21 season. Manchester City won 3-1 at home before the two sides drew 0-0 in this stadium.

Manchester City were busy late on in the transfer window, bringing in both Iliman Ndiaye and Enzo Fernandez as they spent nearly £200m on deadline day alone. They come into tonight’s game off the back of three straight Premier League victories to kick off the Maresca era. Maresca has limited Champions League experience as a manager, which came with Chelsea last season. Manchester City have won their opening game of a Champions League campaign in six of the last seven seasons but this will be the first time since 2015/16 that Manchester City embark on a Champions League campaign without Pep Guardiola at the helm.

“It is a hard place to come [Porto],” said Maresca. “They have started really well. In the last 14/15 games in Europe they lost just one, that shows a difficult place to come, but we will try our best and try to win the game. It is a very, very good team. They have different players, but in terms of the team it is very clear in the way they play. They are aggressive without the ball and on the ball, they have a clear style. But we will try our best and try to win the game. The ambition is the same; try to be ourselves and to win games and then we will see.”

Porto, managed by Francesco Farioli, have won every league game so far this season and already sit four points clear at the summit of Liga Portugal. Farioli takes charge of his first game as a manger in the Champions League and the club make their return to the elite European competition after two seasons away.

“We are going to face one of the big favourites to win the competition,” Farioli said. “It will be a game that will demand that we be at our best, and we know that whenever we step onto the Dragão pitch, something special can happen. I am happy to be in the Champions League for the first time at 37 years old. This will be my first game, but we approach every game with the same attention to detail and the same focus. It is easy for the players to be motivated tomorrow [tonight]. But the key will be our strategy and our ability to execute it, individually and collectively.”

Porto were in the Europa League last season, making it to the quarter-finals, where they were knocked out by Nottingham Forest 2-1 on aggregate. The omens would not appear to be on Porto’s side tonight; they have only won two of their last 16 games against English opposition in major European competition.

Team news from Portugal to follow shortly.

Gianluigi Donnarumma is going through a complicated period. #1555. Michael Carrick is SACKED by Man United: Manager leaves training ground just 2½ hours after arriving - and now Mauricio Pochettino is ready to take over

Published: 05:22 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 07:34 EST, 12 November 2026

Michael Carrick has been sacked by Manchester United, with former Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino waiting in the wings as his successor.

Just 173 days on from Carrick being given a two-year contract, having guided United to a third-placed finish and back into the Champions League as an interim, the decision to fire him was ratified at a crucial board meeting in Monaco on Wednesday.

Carrick arrived at United's training ground at 7.50am this morning and was dismissed. He left at 10.18am, less than two and a half hours later. He is the first Premier League manager to be sacked this season, followed hours later by bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage.

In a statement released at 10.37am, Carrick's sacking was confirmed. United's statement read: 'After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

'Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.'

Sources close to United say the club's leadership believe their squad of players is far better than the performances and results under Carrick have indicated. They gave the under-fire manager a chance to turn things around against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa but ultimately felt the team were not on the right path.

Michael Carrick - pictured arriving at Carrington on Thursday morning - has been sacked after Manchester United's disastrous start to the season

Carrick was seen leaving the training ground less than two and a half hours later

USMNT boss Mauricio Pochettino is ready to take over as United's new manager

Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, along with the Glazer family, who dialled in virtually from the United States, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox reached a verdict in the south of France yesterday, all while Carrick remained in limbo back in Manchester.

Carrick took charge of training on Tuesday morning after it had emerged that Berrada and Wilcox were heading to Monaco to recommend his sacking and did so again on Wednesday when it transpired United were closing in on an agreement to bring in Pochettino as his successor.

The current United States national team manager reached a verbal agreement with Man United to take over on Wednesday. United then made a formal approach to US Soccer shortly after, with the club having to trigger the 54-year-old Argentine's £7million release clause.

The final nail in Carrick’s coffin came in Sunday's dramatic 4-4 draw against Aston Villa, which saw United stuck in the relegation zone in 18th position.

The handling of Carrick’s departure has been particularly damning on Ineos and the shot-callers at United, not least given he was given no show of public support when he continued in post following an emergency board meeting after the 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth.

A defeat at Chelsea, in which Lisandro Martinez badly let his manager down by getting sent off, and a win over Roma to go with the draw against Villa, was not enough of a sign that it will turn around for the board to keep faith.

With Carrick's departure, it pushes the compensation paid out to coaching staff and executives over the last three years under minority owner Ratcliffe and Ineos close to £30million. Buying Pochettino out of his contract with the US national team will cost another £7m. Adding his large coaching staff will take millions more.

Matchgoing supporters will be sad to see Carrick go and made those feelings clear in recent games when he was loudly cheered at the end of matches, with the ire and frustration levelled against players and executives.

Optimism heading into the campaign was sky high given that no team in the Premier League performed better than Carrick's side between January and May.

But that level of success and dominance has long since evaporated after a shambolic start to the current campaign - and it has cost the 45-year-old his job just five months after the ink dried on a new deal.

It has been a season in which United won just three matches, one of which came against Azerbaijani minnows FK Sabah, and are yet to keep a clean sheet in the league all season.

A season in which club captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned his manager's tactics and Martinez eviscerated the hierarchy for hanging Carrick and the players out to dry. Fernandes was even dropped for the first time in five years for the Bournemouth humiliation.

Questions will continue to be asked of those upstairs, with Berrada and Wilcox now on to their third permanent manager this year alone and their fourth in their tenure having burned through Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick since taking control of football operations in February 2024.

It means Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox (pictured on Thursday morning) need a third manager this year as INEOS' running of the football club comes under scrutiny once more

Sunday's draw with Aston Villa proved to be the final nail in the coffin for the United boss

Gary Neville believes Michael Carrick will be 'disgusted' by his Manchester United players

Amorim lasted 14 months in the role, even in spite of embarrassing defeats to the likes of League Two Grimsby Town, but for Carrick it was a dream job that would run until early November and end in him being unceremoniously dumped at the training ground by Wilcox.

Carrick vowed after the Villa draw that he wouldn’t walk away and took on a spiky side when quizzed on his future by reporters. After a week of shame against the board, he has finally been put out of his misery.

Carrick leaves with a record of 14 wins - 12 of which came last season, prior to being made permanent manager - six draws and eight defeats, including exiting this season's Carabao Cup at the first hurdle against Brighton at Old Trafford.

Now it looks set to be Pochettino’s challenge to turn this massively underperforming squad around, something former United star Gary Neville believes is a mightily difficult task given the 'unprofessional' squad the new man will inherit.

'They've teased him, haven't they? They've conned [Carrick] for a few months. They have, they've conned him,' Neville said on his Sky Sports podcast recently.

'Honestly, he would never say this publicly because he's got class. I can say it for him though.

'He'll look at those players with disgust. Some of them, he'll be disgusted with some of those players.

'A few of them aren't that professional. I live in Manchester. Some of them aren't that professional. So I've got no time for them.

'There's a few of them that don't go to bed at the right time, don't eat the right things, don't think about Manchester United every single minute of every day, and aren't living and breathing this football club as they should be - and as professionals should.

'Why? Because it's gone to their heads. They are nothing, some of those players.

'He's not been able to get a tune out of them and they've turned on him. I know that because if Bruno has turned on him publicly, with that little statement, imagine what they're like behind the scenes.

'If that's your captain saying that, imagine what they're saying in the dressing room behind closed doors when no one's listening. That's horrific.'

#1552. Mac Allister not so sad now after Liverpool comeback winner

Do your talking on the pitch, as the old adage goes, and Alexis Mac Allister emphatically did just that as Liverpool came from behind to thrillingly win their first Champions League tie under new head coach Andoni Iraola in what was his debut at this level.

On the eve of this encounter, against a strong Atlético Madrid, one of the clubs who have recently tried to sign him, Mac Allister had spoken of his sadness. Sadness that, unlike fellow midfielders Dominik Szoboszlai – Liverpool’s other scorer here – and Ryan Gravenberch, he had not been offered and signed a new contract.

So, earn it. And many more goals – and overall performances like this – there is no doubt the Argentinian will have a deal placed in front of him. He scored with an arresting second-half shot, which proved to be the winner, and the smile across his face said it all. Not so sad now as he was later substituted to a standing ovation with Gravenberch taking his place.

The goal came early in the second half, with Iraola attributing that to adjusting his tactics after being flummoxed by Atlético’s back five and packed midfield in a first half when Liverpool were second best.

Mac Allister was heavily involved through the build-up, eventually picking out Rio Ngumoha on the left whose shot was blocked and pinballed around. It dropped to Mac Allister, 20 yards out, and he hit the kind of unerring drive that gives the goalkeeper no chance. And so it proved. Boom. And Anfield was bouncing.

Mac Allister FIRES Liverpool into the lead at Anfield! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/KGOvuAEU4W

There are certainly signs under Iraola, and following a difficult last campaign, that Mac Allister is beginning to rediscover the form he showed during his first two seasons at Liverpool. Time and again the 27-year-old made vital interventions, showed aggression and walked the tightrope of a harsh early yellow card. He dovetailed with Szoboszlai and that might be a concern for Gravenberch – watched by the Netherlands’ new head coach Xavi Hernández – if Iraola persists with this approach.

Although Mac Allister has two years left on his current deal, the last thing Liverpool need is yet another attention-sapping contract saga, even if he is not the same scale of player as Mohamed Salah or Trent Alexander-Arnold.

For Iraola, after three Premier League games, comprising two draws and a victory over newly-promoted Ipswich Town, this will hopefully be lift off. A big European night at Anfield and coming from behind to beat one of the continent’s heavyweights.

“I loved it,” Iraola said, before castigating himself for misreading the way Atlético would line up. And what of Mac Allister’s riposte? There was a smile from Iraola before the Spaniard’s usual diplomacy kicked in as he talked about a “lovely, lovely goal” and how good it was for his midfielders to contribute.

Liverpool had to fight for it and what will have satisfied Iraola is that the defence, which has come under such scrutiny, held out. Even so, there are still serious concerns over the suitability of Milos Kerkez at left-back – who was badly at fault for Atlético’s goal – although the robust Ronald Araújo showed he can be a strong and versatile option on the other flank. The Uruguayan, signed on loan from Barcelona, is such a presence in both penalty areas and has the capacity to gain cult status.

As does £123m signing from Paris St-Germain Bradley Barcola, who should have scored – once, certainly, possibly twice – and possesses astonishing pace that will undoubtedly lead to goals. There are also encouraging signs that his presence could enliven Florian Wirtz. Barcola eventually also went off, but thankfully it was only to cramp.

There was a collective intake of breath across the Kop when Marcos Llorente was played through and bore down on them to give Atlético the lead. There was a desperate hope that he had strayed offside. There was then a realisation that Kerkez had, however, played him on with an appalling lack of awareness. Llorente beat Alisson.

It owed much to a wonderful shimmy, deceiving Szoboszlai in centre field, by Julián Alvarez before he smartly threaded the ball through, and Mac Allister’s international team-mate almost doubled Atlético’s advantage soon after. Only to be denied by Alisson.

Llorente breaks the deadlock! 🔥That's now FIVE Champions League goals for the Atletico man against Liverpool at Anfield 🤯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Rxp4zurfpc

We knew, we feared it would be Llorente who scored. Remarkably, he has now half of his 10 goals in this competition against Liverpool. Indeed, he named his dog Anfield after his extra-time brace knocked Liverpool, then the holders, out in the last 16 in 2020. And Liverpool had made a dog’s dinner of defending this time.

This is a different Atlético. A far less defensive, far more expansive Atlético. In years gone by, once they were 1-0 it was game over under Diego Simeone. But these days they try and play more and that gives their opponents a chance. And so it proved.

Atlético goalkeeper Jan Oblak did well to deny Barcola, with his trailing foot, before Wirtz won the ball back and found Szoboszlai who eventually ended the movement. It owed much, however, to a clever backheel to pick out the midfielder who finished low into the corner. Who executed that backheel? That would be Araújo.

Szoboszlai slots home after a brilliant flick from Araujo! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UrHQTwtgsY

Barcola should have scored, sent clear by Wirtz in a brilliant, sweeping counter-attack, before Mac Allister did.

The question now was whether Liverpool would show the resilience to see through the result. As Iraola made changes, they answered that with a resounding yes, which will have pleased him as much as the result, as much as the comeback, as much as Mac Allister’s stunning response.

“I was enjoying it [the Anfield crowd]. They [Atletico Madrid] are a very good team. Technically, in the middle, lovely players. It is not easy to press those players as they have quality. They have been playing together forever. We find another comeback after Nottingham Forest, after Newcastle. We still have this thing to improve in the beginning of the games, but I am happy as we have shown some character. This is the Champions League, you do not have easy games.”

"You can see he's football mad." ⚽Steven Gerrard on Andoni Iraola's passion and the impact he's making at Liverpool 👏🎙️ @laura_woodsy | 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/M3qKhxt8HE
