Atletico had more possession in the second half but Liverpool were much the better side after the break.

"We can achieve everything we want." 💪Dominik Szoboszlai full of belief after Liverpool's Champions League victory over Atletico Madrid 👀🎙️ @jules_breach | 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ebSvagW4yx

There is the final whistle at Anfield and Liverpool start their Champions League campaign with a 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid. Liverpool did fall behind to Marcos Llorente’s goal but goals from Dominik Szoboszlai and Alexis Mac Allister give Andoni Iraola a win in his first Champions League game as a manager.

Victory in MD1 🤩 #UCL pic.twitter.com/SWFFhSudFJ

First Champions League game. First Champions League win for Andoni Iraola ✅ pic.twitter.com/D3CE6w6V0b

Koumas is tripped by Le Normand and that should be it.

That is a silly foul from Lookman, with Frimpong inside his own box running back towards his own goal, but Lookman decides to push him in the back.

Liverpool think they have sealed it through Frimpong but the offside flag has gone up. First Munoz cuts onto his right and has a shot saved by Oblak. The ball falls to Frimpong, who slots home but he was clearly offside when Munoz took the initial shot.

Kerkez is currently down with cramp and his night is done. He will be replaced by Tsimikas and Liverpool will make their final change at the same time. Koumas comes on for Isak.

Atletico win a corner but it all stems from sloppy play in the centre of the pitch from Gravenberch. He has had a few sloppy moments since coming on.

The corner is flicked on by Hjulmand but ends up coming to nothing.

It isn’t the headline making performance, by any means, but that shouldn’t dilute the importance of Ronald Araujo’s contribution for Liverpool tonight and, indeed, against Ipswich last Friday. He’s doing what Liverpool wanted him to, providing versatility and leadership in their back four and - more than anything - quality. He hasn’t put a foot wrong.

Atletico win a corner out on the left in front of their travelling supporters. Grimaldo’s outswinger is flicked on by the head of Hancko at the near post but it goes over.

Isak has the chance to potentially seal the victory for Liverpool but Le Normand makes a crucial block. Le Normand has only just come on but already made a couple of defensive actions.

Liverpool win a corner out on the left with the last touch coming off Pubill, who was marking Van Dijk from a free-kick. Szoboszlai’s inswinger is headed away by Le Normand.

Digeo Simeone is making his final two substitutions of the night as Le Normand and Hjulmad replace Romero and Barrios,

Atletico bring on David, on loan from Juventus, for Baena.

Alvarez has a chance inside the Liverpool box but his shot is straight at Alisson. There are some appeals for handball but it hit Munoz from such close range that it is never a penalty.

Liverpool are making a substitution as Mac Allister, who scored the goal to put Liverpool in front, is replaced by Gravenberch. Mac Allister, who made some comments in the press conference yesterday about his sadness at not being offered a new contract, put in a good performance in the centre of Liverpool’s midfield. He was on a booking though so probably sensible to take him off when you can guarantee that the Atletico players would have tried to get him sent off.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks and months but there have been glimmers here with Florian Wirtz looking better than he has done with pace to pass to; if it clicks with him, Bradley Barcola & Alexander Isak it could be exciting but one game must be built on. It’s frustrating that Barcola’s night has ended with what appears to be cramp or tightness in his calf because he was getting more joy than he had done before half-time. The big challenge for Liverpool, too, is whether they have the nous to see this contest out.

The new Netherlands boss Xavi is in attendance at Anfield tonight, watching the likes of Van Dijk, Frimpong and Gravenberch, although the latter is still yet to come off the Liverpool bench.

This is a concern for Liverpool. Barcola has gone down and seems to have some pain in his left calf. Is it cramp or an injury? It will be a double change for the home side as Frimpong and Munoz come on. Barcola is given a standing ovation as he goes off and the Liverpool fans will be hoping it is just cramp. Ngumoha also heads off.

Diego Simeone is going to make his first two changes of the night. Grimaldo and Lookman come on

It is all Liverpool as they sense a third goal is there for the taking. Ngumoha does well down Liverpool’s left and pushes it past Pubill, who slides in and takes him down. Pubill is booked. He cannot believe it but I do not know why; a clear foul and yellow card.

That is a stunning strike from the Argentine. The ball falls to the midfielder just outside the box and he hits it first time. He hits the ball so crisply and there is nothing Oblak can do to stop it. Liverpool should have taken the lead through Barcola moments before they do now have the lead for the first time tonight.

Mac Allister FIRES Liverpool into the lead at Anfield! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/KGOvuAEU4W

Well, that’s one way to prove you might warrant a new contract. A quite beautiful left footed drive from Alexis Mac Allister gives Liverpool the lead and it has been noticeable thus far in Andoni Iraola’s matches that his team get stronger at the start of the second period. Diego Simeone most wonder how Atleti are losing a game they were controlling but Liverpool’s speed on the break is proving very good at causing chaos.

Barcola should have his first Liverpool goal and the hosts should be ahead but the Frenchman misses the target. It is the perfect counter-attack really from Liverpool and it is Wirtz and Barcola who exchange passes from deep inside their own half all the way to the Atletico penalty area. Barcola drives forward, into the Atletico box, and you think he is going to slot it into the bottom corner but his effort goes just wide. Barcola could and perhaps should have a brace tonight.

Barcola wins the first corner of this second half off Hancko right in front of The Kop. Liverpol take it short before Mac Allister clips the ball in. Araujo meets it and his header is powerful but it is off target.

We are back under way at Anfield. No changes from either side at the break.

Some of the statistics are pretty even but Atletico Madrid have had just three touches in the Liverpool penalty area, yet have a goal to their name.

The first half at Anfield is brought to an end and it is level at 1-1 at the break. Llorente gave Atletico the lead before Szoboszlai equalised for Liverpool. The home fans let the officials know what they think of their performance in that first half.

One added minute at the end of this first half.

There has been about five minutes of squabbling between the Liverpool and Atletico benches, so much so that Tommy Elphick - Andoni Iraola’s assistant - missed Dominik Szoboszlai score the equaliser. Tensions have only increased after a nasty little challenge from Cristian Romero on Alexander Isak. The half-time whistle might be coming at a good time to defuse the situation but you fancy the walk back to the dressing rooms will be spicy.

The conduct of the Atletico players is frankly embarrassing, not a massive surprise from a Diego Simeone side. Kang goes down clutching his face when there was barely any contact and then, unlike Isak, he does not have to spend a minute off the pitch.

Isak is on the ground, clutching at his knee, after a heavy challenge from Romero. It is a nasty challenge from Romero, who remarkably is neither booked nor penalised. To compound the awful officiating, Isak now has to spend a minute off the pitch owing to the new rules. What do you make of that new rule of the player who is down going off for a minute? Have your say in the comments section at the bottom of the blog.

Moments after Liverpool equalised, Atletico have a decent opportunity to restore their lead but Baena drags his effort wide from the edge of the box.

Moments after Barcola could not take a big chance to equalise for Liverpool, Szoboslzai does. First, Barcola is denied by Oblak. Liverpool keep it alive inside the Atletico box and a simple sensational flick by Aruajo finds Szoboszlai, who finds the bottom corner with a clinical finish. Kerkez has been poor tonight but he deserves credit for his part in that goal as he was the player to initially win it back for Liverpool with a good press.

Szoboszlai slots home after a brilliant flick from Araujo! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UrHQTwtgsY

Liverpool look like a team that has been out of the Champions League for a couple of years and are only just finding its feet, which seems strange given they missed only one year in the last 10. They have glimmers of promise but they aren’t convincing anyone they will blow Atleti’s house down. One day everything will align for Atleti and they will reach another final. They have an outside chance this year, especially if Julian Alvarez - easily the best player on this pitch - has anything to do with it. Diego Simeone always has class strikers at the top of his team and Alvarez stands comparison with any who have gone before.

Wirtz has a great chance to equalise for Liverpool but his shot on the half volley is saved by Oblak. It would not have mattered anyway had the ball ended up in the net because Isak was offside before crossing for Wirtz.

Some of the officiating tonight has been appalling and the latest example is VAR taking a check on a possible red card for Mac Allister for a foul that is never a red card in a million years. The officials then take an age to give yet another obvious offside and, in the end, the referee gives it rather than the linesman. That really does sum up the officials tonight as the referee should not be the one to give offsides.

Alvarez shoots from distance and forces Alisson into a good save diving to his right. There was a suspicion of offside from Simeone in the build-up.

Atletico take it short but Simeone’s shot is blocked by Araujo.

What a save from Alisson! 🤯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/PuajED3Rks

The Anfield faithful are furious. Two fouls in quick succession are not given when they were both clearly fouls. The referee appears to have a different interpretation of body checks and taking people out off the ball than the rest of us.

The Spanish side take the lead at Anfield and it is another goal on this ground for Llorente. Alvarez feeds a through ball to pick out the run of Llorente, who is onside. He takes one touch before firing past Alisson from the edge of the box. That is poor, poor defending from Kerkez, who not only played Llorente onside but then did not track the run properly. Llorente now has five goals on this ground.

Llorente breaks the deadlock! 🔥That's now FIVE Champions League goals for the Atletico man against Liverpool at Anfield 🤯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Rxp4zurfpc

The idea that Atletico Madrid are focused on spoiling and nullifying belongs in the past. They are an attractive team, well organised and you suspect they have the gears to cause Liverpool problems... and as we type, they have just opened the scoring by playing straight through Liverpool’s middle. It was a bad goal for home side to concede. Milos Kerkez was out of sync with the rest of Liverpool’s defence and Marcos Llorente has galloped straight through. As we said at the start: it’s a big test for the hosts... it’s just got even bigger.

A little line about Llorente, who has now scored five times against Liverpool in the Champions League. He is fond of playing in this arena, he named his dog “Anfield! when he bought it in 2021.

Chance for Barcola. Szoboszlai clips a lovely ball in behind down the right channel to pick out the run of Barcola. The Frenchman takes it down beautifully before having his shot saved by Oblak. Barcola’s best moment thus far tonight.

Baena takes a first-time effort on from a central position around 25 yards out but he cannot keep his effort down and it sails into The Kop.

Atletico were renowned for years under Diego Simeone is being very tight at the back and in midfield, especially away from home. However, in recent years they have become more expansive and as a result are more open.

Liverpool win their first corner of the night at the Anfield Road End in front of the travelling Atletico fans. They take it short and Szoboslzai takes it towards the Atletico box. It appeared to be a very obvious foul on Szoboszlai right on the edge of the box but nothing is given. At the very least, it should have been given a free-kick as there was definitely at least one foul.

Barcola, who has won the Champions League with PSG in the last two seasons, is starting out on the right for Liverpool tonight with Ngumoha on the left.

Big test for Liverpool and it will be fascinating to see how this formation works out. It looks very much like it is 4-4-2, with Florian Wirtz almost alongside Alexander Isak and Rio Ngumoha the left winger and Bradley Barcola on the opposite flank - a position Andoni Iraola has referenced him playing in Lyon as a teenager. It’s also a big test for Iraola against Diego Simeone, the wily and vastly experienced manager, who is immaculately dressed - as always - in his trademark black suit.

Liverpool have a chance inside the opening minute. Szoboszlai wins it inside his own half and drives forward. He then plays it out to his right to find Isak, whose shot from the right side of the box is dragged wide of the far post. Isak did score from a similar position against Ipswich last Friday, when he scored at the near post.

A minute’s silence to remember the victims of the landslides in Nepal is impeccably observed.

We are under way at Anfield. Liverpool’s Champions League campaign gets going as Andoni Iraola takes charge of his first game as a manager in this competition.

The two sides emerge from the tunnel to a cacophony of noise and we are moments away from kick-off at Anfield. The home fans boo the Champions League anthem and belt out “Liverpool! Liverpool!” over the top of it. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

The original “This is Anfield” sign has sold at auction for almost £150,000, 10 times more than its guide price.

The sign that hung above the players’ tunnel at Liverpool’s home stadium during the 1970s had been expected to fetch between £10,000 and £15,000 after being put up for auction on Tuesday and Wednesday.

But the “talismanic” piece of football memorabilia ended up being sold by auctioneer Budds for £149,500 to a UK private buyer.

The Argentine is into the final two years of his contract, which runs out in 2028. He arrived at Liverpool in the same summer as fellow midfielders Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai, who have both signed new contracts. Mac Allister was linked with a move away from Liverpool during the summer transfer window and was candid about his contractual situation in the press conference yesterday:

“I received the news that the club was not in a position to offer me a new contract which, of course, makes me very, very sad. Everyone can see that I give my 100% for this football club every single day in training and games. Of course, I can have very good games [and] bad games, like everyone, but I always give my best.

“I see Dominik [Szoboszlai] and Ryan [Gravenberch] renewing their contracts and that makes me very happy because they deserve it. At the same time it makes me a little bit sad that I did not get mine. Of course, there is still time. The fans do not need to worry because I will give my 100% until the last day I am here. There were options to leave this summer. I think right now I am in the right club and I have the right mindset to give 100% for this club.”

Former Liverpool manager Rafa Benitez, who led the club to Champions League glory on that famous night in Istanbul in 2005, is in attendance tonight. Andoni Iraola has just shared a hug with his compatriot and perhaps Benitez will have a few words of advice for Iraola ahead of his Champions League debut as a manager.

The Dutchman has been in fine form at the start of the season for Liverpool, registering a goal and three assists in his first three games. He missed training yesterday and is not in Liverpool’s matchday squad tonight. Andoni Iraola has confirmed that Gakpo has a small adductor injury that he picked up in the Ipswich game last Friday but could be fit for the weekend against Fulham.

When Liverpool won their sixth European Cup in 2019, they lifted it in the Wanda Metropolitano against Tottenham. This season’s Champions League final is in that very stadium and Liverpool’s Champions League campaign starts tonight against the club that plays their home games in that stadium, Atletico Madrid.

“This is going to be a challenge, I hope, all the season because it would mean we continue in all the competitions. In this case, it is not the worst scenario because we played last Friday so we have had I think a good recovery. Probably it is going to be more difficult for next weekend, especially for the next game against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup because we will have just two days, game, two days, game. But we have to get used to this; it is what big clubs do. Definitely there is part of your mind where you have to think [about] the next games. But for us, the game tomorrow is very important.”

Ready for #UCL action 👊🔴 pic.twitter.com/XyOupLwsRe

Liverpool begin their Champions League campaign at home as they host Atletico Madrid at Anfield. These sides met at Anfield on matchday one last season, with Liverpool winning a dramatic game 3-2. Liverpool led 2-0 inside the opening 10 minutes before Atletico came back to level the game at 2-2. Virgil van Dijk then scored in added time to give Liverpool all three points before Atletico boss Diego Simeone was sent off for clashing with the Anfield crowd, resulting in a one-match ban.

Andoni Iraola earned his first win as Liverpool boss on Friday night as they won 2-0 away at Ipswich thanks to a quickfire early double from Alexander Isak. This will be Iraola’s first Champions League match as a manager.

“I think obviously it is a special night for me,” Iraola said. “Everyone talks [about] the Champions League nights at Anfield and also the first game is against a strong opposition, it is Atletico Madrid. [Diego] Simeone is doing an incredible job as a manager. To be all the years that he has been achieving every season the goals of the club I think is remarkable and definitely it is a big challenge for us. I think I played against him as a player, he was still a player, and I played against his teams when he was a coach and I also coached against him. So, we had a lot of precedent before. Definitely he has much more experience than me in this kind of games but I hope tomorrow we can give him a good game.

“It is one of the dreams, probably, when you start. It was difficult for me when I started my coaching career seven, eight years ago, to position myself in the position that I am right now, and I hope I can enjoy it. It is a big responsibility, massive challenge, but I feel privileged to be there in that dugout tomorrow [tonight] and now my thinking is about putting the team together in a position where we can play a good game, win the game and start strong in this Champions League.”

Atletico Madrid currently sit sixth in La Liga and suffered their first defeat on Saturday as they lost 3-0 at Athletic Bilbao. They did reach the semi-finals of the Champions League last season, where they fell to Arsenal 2-1 on aggregate.

“We are coming into a marvellous stadium and there will be a great atmosphere,” Simeone said. “We will have to look good from the start of the game because it will be full on. He [Andoni Iraola] works very well with the team, focusing on the tactical awareness of each player. It takes time to find the right path, but he is growing and improving and he has some very good players.”

Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1550. Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage after disastrous 16-game spell - this is how his reign unravelled over late, intense sessions, dinner at the training ground and an unpopular assistant manager

Published: 10:17 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 07:52 EST, 12 November 2026

Crystal Palace have sacked Pierre Sage after players and club chiefs grew frustrated over his training methods, Daily Mail Sport can reveal.

A 3-1 defeat by Liverpool on Sunday saw Palace drop to bottom of the Premier League for the first time in nine years and proved to be the final straw for club bosses.

Daily Mail Sport understands that while the Palace players got on well with the 47-year-old, they were frustrated by his late training sessions – with some not starting until 4pm. The regimented routine required players to stay at the training ground for dinner on the night before matches, with some not returning home until 8pm ahead of a 2pm kick-off the following day.

The club's hierarchy, meanwhile, expressed concerns early in the Frenchman's tenure that he was not doing enough defensive work on the training pitch.

Sage's philosophy was that the best way to defend was having the ball, meaning training sessions focused on running, pressing and possession rather than defensive structure.

But the lack of focus led to a poor defensive record, with Palace conceding 30 goals in 16 matches across all competitions. Defending set-pieces and counter-attacks has been a persistent problem for Sage’s side, and he won just two of his ten Premier League games in charge.

Pierre Sage has been sacked by Crystal Palace after a dismal start to the season saw them win just two of their first ten games

Palace sit rock bottom of the Premier League, their leaky defence having conceded 24 goals

Daily Mail Sport understands many players voiced fears they were being pushed too hard in training, with sessions the day before a game particularly intense. There were also significant concerns about the quality of Sage's backroom staff, with his assistant Jamal Alioui proving especially unpopular among the players.

There has also been considerable turnover among senior executives, with six departures over the past 18 months. Chief financial officer Mitesh Velani is set to add to that number in the coming months. One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that the disruption to the club’s business operations has the hallmarks of a club heading for relegation.

As Palace look to bail themselves out of trouble, Daily Mail Sport understands talks are progressing with former Brentford and Tottenham boss Thomas Frank, who is expected to take over ahead of crucial games against Coventry and Hull after the international break.

Palace chairman Steve Parish first contemplated sacking Sage over his lack of defensive nous in September, but gave him a stay of execution after Palace kept a clean sheet in a spirited performance away at Leeds on the eve of the international break. However, that display proved an anomaly as Palace shipped 19 goals in the following nine games.

Palace have won just once in their last eight matches in all competitions, beating Fulham 1-0 in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

In September, Daily Mail Sport revealed tensions had emerged between Sage and Parish when the latter took a dim view of the decision to drop teenage defender Jaydee Canvot for their defeat by Ipswich Town.

Palace paid French club RC Lens £4million in compensation to appoint Sage in June after he won the French Cup, finished second in Ligue 1 behind Paris Saint-Germain and was named manager of the season last term. It was the first time in 10 years that Palace had paid compensation to appoint a manager.

Palace chairman Steve Parish (right) first contemplated dismissing Sage in September over a lack of defensive nous

Palace players found Sage’s training sessions too intense and struggled to adapt to the late schedule

Succeeding Oliver Glasner, Palace's greatest manager, proved too big a task for Sage.

Following Palace's loss to Liverpool, Sage insisted the Eagles have been playing better than their league position suggests and pleaded for more time. Those appeals fell on deaf ears.

'A lot of times I’ve said we deserved better and it was the case again (on Sunday),' said Sage. 'My job is not the most important thing, as I always said from the beginning. The most important thing is to find an efficient solution for the team and for the club.

‘I know how important it is for the club to stay in the Premier League. The club just have to believe in (me), and if it's not the case, they will take a decision. I always have confidence in myself because it's a big, big mistake to not be 100 per cent involved in what I have to do.

‘We have to adjust some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions and more efficiency and I think it will be OK.’

#1549. A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1,2,3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

Insect pests cause losses to crop production and damage vegetation4,5. During feeding, insects release oral secretions containing proteins and other molecules that can activate or suppress host plant defence6,7,8. Digestive enzymes hydrolyse cellular components to generate nutrients for herbivores. These breakdown products also act as host-derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that activate plant pattern-recognition receptors9,10. Identifying host-derived signalling molecules and their defence activation mechanisms is essential for developing new plant-protection strategies.

T2-family ribonuclease (RNaseT2) proteins, which preferentially cleave single-strand RNAs between purine and uridine residues, are ancient enzymes that are widely distributed across organisms and functional in diverse biological processes2,11. Plant S-RNases, which mediate self-incompatibility, belong to this protein family12. Phytopathogens also secrete nucleases into host tissues13,14. Human lysosomal RNaseT2 generates purine-2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated oligoribonucleotides that are sensed by Toll-like receptor 8 to activate innate immunity2. Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domains of plant intracellular nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors possess enzymatic activities towards oxidized nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and nucleic acids15,16,17,18,19. Plant TIR domains generate second messengers such as 2′-ADPR and pRib-AMP, which promote the formation of EDS1–Phytoalexin Deficient 4 (PAD4)–Activated Disease Resistance 1 (ADR1) complex and trigger disease resistance15,20,21. Activated plant TIR also catalyses the production of ADPr-ATP and di-ADPR, leading to the complex formation of EDS1-Senescence-Associated Gene 101 (SAG101)–N Required Gene 1 (NRG1), inducing plant cell death16,22,23. Plant TIR domains also synthesize 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP (2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP) through nuclease activity. Arabidopsis nudix hydrolase 7 (AtNUDT7) hydrolyses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and attenuates TIR-mediated cell death when overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana3. However, the contribution of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP to EDS1-dependent immunity remains elusive.

Plant glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins (GRPs) encompassing one RNA recognition motif (RRM) at the N terminus and a glycine-rich region (GRR) at the C terminus regulate plant responses to abiotic and biotic stresses24,25. Arabidopsis GRP7 (AtGRP7) has a positive role in immunity, whereas the Pseudomonas syringae effector HopU1 suppresses AtGRP7-mediaed immunity by catalysing ADP-ribosylation of an arginine residue (R49) in the RRM of AtGRP726,27,28. These data indicate that the RRM of GRPs is central to immune function, although the underlying molecular mechanism remains unidentified. Here we report that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading insect T2 RNases (such as NVR1) to promote ribonuclease activity and the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p. Binding to the cyclic nucleotides via RMM stimulates NIB1 phase separation to assemble the plant defence machinery in the nucleus.

Nezara viridula (the green stink bug) is a polyphagous hemipteran pest feeding on a wide range of plants, including economically important food, fruit and vegetable crops and Nicotiana species. Populations of N. viridula have recently increased in rice fields. As a piercing-sucking mesophyll feeder (Fig. 1a), N. viridula uses needle-like stylets to puncture developing seeds or young leaves, extract nutrients and inject effectors29. To identify the secretory enzymes, we profiled proteins in its oral secretions using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) and identified 22 putative digestive enzymes, of which 15 were likely to be secretory based on signal peptide prediction (SignalP 3.0 server) and de-redundancy (Blastp) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Transient expression of these proteins in N. benthamiana leaves identified one candidate enzyme that induced severe cell death and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production within 3 days post-agroinfiltration (dpi) (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). This protein shows high sequence similarity to ribonuclease and we named it N. viridula ribonuclease 1 (NVR1).

a, Fifth-instar nymph of N. viridula on rice panicle (left) and the adult on kidney beans (right). b, Diagram of NVR1 showing the N-terminal signal peptide (amino acids 1 to 24) predicted by Signalp 3.0 and the nuclease catalytic region (amino acids 28 to 235) predicted by Pfam. NVR1 was predicted to have an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and no transmembrane region. Analysis using the protein family database (Pfam) revealed a ribonuclease (RNase) domain (Fig. 1b) that belongs to the RNaseT2 family11. NVR1 was detected both in N. viridula salivary glands and in infested rice plants, suggesting that it is secreted into plant tissues during feeding (Extended Data Fig. 1d). NVR1 exhibited a nucleocytoplasmic distribution pattern (Extended Data Fig. 1e).

H64 and H116 are conserved among T2 RNases from mammals, herbivorous insects, phytopathogenic fungi and plants (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1f). NVR1 cleaved Cy5-labelled Arabidopsis tRNASer (83 nt) in vitro, whereas NVR1(H116A) and NVR1(H64A) mutants showed mild and strong reductions in substrate degradation, respectively, and the double mutant NVR1(H-doub) was almost completely inactivated (Fig. 1d), supporting H64 and H116 as key catalytic residues11. High-resolution mass spectrometry was subsequently used to identify products of the NVR1-catalysed reaction, which showed accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP, as well as a dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate with a mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of 675.1072 in positive mode (Fig. 1e,f). Given that preferentially cleavage of single-stranded RNA between purines and uridines by RNaseT2 produces guanosine or adenosine 2′,3′-cyclophosphate termini2, we designed two oligoribonucleotides, (UAGU)5 and (UGAU)5, as substrates to determine the structure of the product. NVR1 exhibited activity towards (UAGU)5—but not towards (UGAU)5—generating a peak at 5.1 min in the extracted ion chromatogram mode that was identical to the dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate peak at m/z 675.1072, suggesting that NVR1 produced 2′,3′-cGMP-terminated AMP (ApG>p). The ApG>p synthetic standard, eluting at 5.1 min with a m/z of 675.1072 in positive mode, aligns with the NVR1 product (Fig. 1f) and matches the tandem mass (MS2) spectrum (Extended Data Fig. 1g). The accumulation of 2′,3′- cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P was rapidly induced in rice leaves within 2 h after insect feeding (Fig. 1g).

The 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p synthase activity of NVR1 was dependent on the two catalytic histidines H64 and H116 (Fig. 1h). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)–mass spectrometry and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) analysis showed that N. benthamiana leaves expressing empty vector or catalytic inactive NVR1 mutants accumulated much less 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than leaves expressing wild-type NVR1 (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Leaves expressing NVR1 mutants were impaired in inducing plant cell death (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1i). AtNUDT7 hydrolysed 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (Fig. 1k). Co-expression with AtNUDT7 attenuated cell death activity of NVR1 in N. benthamiana at 3 dpi, with necrosis completed at 6 dpi (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 1j,k). These results indicate that the NVR1 enzymatic activity was causative to plant cell death.

To investigate plant responses to pest RNase, we generated rice NVR1-GFP transgenic plants that overexpress NVR1–GFP (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed that genes associated with biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence were significantly enriched in NVR1-expressing plants (Extended Data Fig. 2c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d) were upregulated and levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid levels increased (Extended Data Fig. 2e). The Cnaphalocrocis medinalis ribonuclease 1 (CMR1), an NVR1 orthologue expressed by Cnaphalocrocis medinalis—a lepidopteran pest of rice—was detected in oral secretions and also produced 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g), congruent with the rice leaf-feeding data (Fig. 1g). Given this functional conservation, we evaluated the resistance of NVR1 transgenic lines to C. medinalis. The larvae gained less weight on NVR1-expressing plants than on controls (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Adult females laid fewer eggs on NVR1 transgenic lines, and larvae preferred feeding on control plants (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j).

NVR1-expressing plants were stunted and produced fewer tillers, phenotypes associated with the growth cost of constitutive defence activation, whereas rice plants expressing catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub) did not upregulate defence genes and grew normally (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). These results demonstrate that heterologous expression of NVR1 in rice elicited defence responses and enhanced plant resistance to insect feeding, and that NVR1 catalytic activity is essential for immune activation.

To uncover the molecular mechanisms underpinning the NVR1-induced plant defence response, we screened plant proteins that could bind to NVR1 by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (IP–MS). NVR1-interacting RNA-binding protein 1 (NIB1 (Os03t0670700-04), also known as OsGRP330,31) showed a strong interaction signal (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). NIB1 is a GRP composed of an N-terminal RRM and a C-terminal GRR and shares 80% N-terminal sequence identity with AtGRP726,27 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Microscale thermophoresis (MST) indicated that NIB1 interacted directly with NVR1 in vitro (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3d), and co-immunoprecipitation confirmed the interaction in planta (Fig. 2b).

Split luciferase complementation (SLC) showed that the NIB1 RRM, but not the GRR, interacted with NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 3e), matching the MST data (Fig. 2a). AlphaFold2 predicted the RRM residue R22 as a contact site (Extended Data Fig. 3f), and the NIB1(R22A) mutant abolished the interaction in planta (Extended Data Fig. 3g). NVR1 interacted strongly with NIB1, independently of its catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 3h–j).

Given that NVR1-like secretory T2 ribonucleases are widespread in insects and phytopathogenic fungi (Extended Data Fig. 1f), and GRPs are conserved across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3k), we investigated whether the RNaseT2–GRP interaction is a common phenomenon. We tested secreted RNases T2 from the insect pests C. medinalis (CMR1) and Helicoverpa armigera (HAR1) and the fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae (MOR1). SLC assays demonstrated that the recognition of T2-family RNases by plant GRPs is universal (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m).

Given that GRPs bind RNA fragments27 and NVR1 requires its RNase activity to elicit defence, we investigated the potential binding of NIB1 to the RNaseT2 products. NIB1–GST was incubated with NVR1 products, denatured to extract the bound molecules, and analysed by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Notably, high-intensity signals of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p were observed (Fig. 2c). Structural modelling of NIB1 with ligands identified two adjoining residues in RRM domain loop, R49 and G50 that were responsible for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP recognition (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). R49 is a known RNA-binding site27, whereas G50 contacts both 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP in our model. G14 and W17 serve as additional recognition sites for ApG>p (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). In MST assays with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, NHS-labelled NIB1 exhibited high binding affinity. Substitution of either residue with alanine (NIB1(R49A) or NIB1(G50A)) markedly reduced the binding affinity, and the NIB1(R49A/G50A/G14A/W17A) (hereafter NIB1(4A)) mutation fully abolished the ApG>p binding (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). G14, W17, R49 and G50 are highly conserved in a group of GRPs across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3n), implying a critical role of these residues in ligand recognition. The NIB1(R49A) mutation impaired NIB1 binding to both RNA and 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides, whereas the NIB1(G50A) mutant maintained binding affinity towards FLAGELLIN SENSITIVE2 (FLS2) 3′ untranslated region (UTR) while showing strongly impaired binding to 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Thus, NIB1 employs shared yet distinct recognition mechanisms for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and RNA.

In MST assays using 2′,3′-cAMP as a positive control, NIB1 did not bind 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP or 2′,3′-cGAMP32 (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g). NIB1 exhibited 4-fold and 34-fold weaker binding affinities for 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP, respectively, compared with 2′,3′-cGMP (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4h,i).

NIB1 contains a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Extended Data Fig. 5a) that mediates phase separation33. PONDR predicted a high average disorder score similar to that of AtGRP7 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). In vitro, NIB1–YFP formed droplets that showed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and fused to form larger droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5c–e). NIB1–YFP signals also recovered after photobleaching in N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 5f).

To determine whether herbivory induces NIB1 condensation in planta, we generated two pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice lines (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Following 6 h of feeding by third-instar C. medinalis larvae, distinct NIB1 nuclear condensates were clearly visualized (Fig. 2f), indicating that this phase separation is a physiologically relevant response to herbivory. Similar to the observations in vitro and in N. benthamiana nuclei, NIB1–YFP condensates in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 nuclei recovered fluorescence after photobleaching (Extended Data Fig. 5h).

We further analysed the interplay between NVR1 catalytic activity and NIB1 condensation. Wild-type NIB1–YFP, but not the C-terminal IDR-truncated NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP, absorbed NVR1–mCherry into the droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). The droplets of purified NIB1–YFP protein with nucleic acid contamination, but not that of nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, were enlarged in the presence of NVR1–mCherry, whereas the catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub)–mCherry did not exert such effect (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). NIB1–YFP exhibited nucleoplasmic localization, and NVR1 significantly enhanced its nuclear accumulation, with about 70% of the examined nuclei containing distinct condensates. N-terminal YFP-tagged NIB1 showed a similar localization pattern (Extended Data Fig. 5l–n). Immunoblotting further confirmed that NVR1 promoted nuclear accumulation of NIB1 (Extended Data Fig. 5o). Nuclear condensates were not observed for the NIB1–NVR1(H-doub) or NIB1(ΔIDR)–NVR1 (Fig. 2g), revealing that the RNase activity of NVR1 is crucial for promoting NIB1 phase separation in the nucleus. In subsequent analyses, we focused on nuclear NIB1 condensates.

Multivalent interactions drive phase separation and locally concentrate molecules, as in dsDNA-dependent cGAS activation and NAD+/ATP-dependent plant TIR activation32,34. We investigated whether 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p would induce NIB1 phase separation. The NIB1(R49A)–YFP and NIB1(G50A)–YFP droplets were smaller than NIB1–YFP droplets with or without NVR1–mCherry (Extended Data Fig. 6a). When co-expressed with NVR1 in N. benthamiana, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) did not generate sparkling nuclear condensates (Extended Data Fig. 6b), implying that NIB1 phase separation involves binding of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p. Congruently, 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p (2 nM each) promoted NIB1 phase separation in vitro (Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d), and treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP or ApG>p increased nuclear condensates in N. benthamiana cells (Fig. 2i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6e). Notably, exogenous application of 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p for 6 h induced distinct nuclear condensates in the pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice plant (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 6f), indicating that 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p act as agonists of NIB1 in promoting phase separation.

We further monitored NIB1–YFP condensation in N. benthamiana leaves upon treatment with nucleotide analogues. Consistent with findings from MST (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g), 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP and 2′3′-cGAMP did not trigger condensate formation, whereas 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP induced far fewer condensates than 2′,3′-cAMP (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h). Co-incubation with NVR1, rice plant RNA (OsRNA) and 2′,3′-cAMP resulted in larger NIB1–YFP droplets in vitro, which required the NVR1 catalytic activity, NIB1 binding sites and 2′,3′-cAMP to achieve optimal effect (Extended Data Fig. 6i). In vitro reconstitutions revealed that NIB1–YFP formed droplets, dependent on 2′,3′-cAMP, OsRNA and salt, as well as protein and macromolecular crowding agent concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 6j–m).

To investigate the biochemical consequences of NIB1 liquid–liquid phase separation, we examined its effect on NVR1 enzymatic activity. NVR1 was more active in the presence of NIB1, and the substrate degradation increased with higher concentrations of NIB1 (Fig. 3a). When the C-terminal IDR-containing fragment was deleted (NIB1(ΔIDR)), the influence of NIB1 on NVR1 activity was reduced or negligible (Fig. 3b), suggesting that the IDR steers NIB1 to boost the NVR1 enzymatic activity. Consistently, the NVR1–NIB1 complex synthesized a higher amount of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than NVR1 alone, which also required the IDR in NIB1 for increased activity (Fig. 3c). Similarly, when co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves, full-length NIB1 significantly enhanced NVR1 in generating 2′,3′-cNMP compared with NIB1(ΔIDR) (Extended Data Fig. 6n). We subsequently evaluated the effect of NIB1 on NVR1-induced cell death in N. benthamiana and found that removing the IDR from NIB1 largely abrogated its potentiation of NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). Additionally, the NIB1(R49A) and NIB1(G50A) mutants also showed compromised acceleration of NVR1 catalysis (Fig. 3d) and the NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6q,r). In sum, catalytically active NVR1 stimulates NIB1 phase separation, which in turn enhances NVR1 activity in degrading RNA and synthesizing 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, thereby inducing plant cell death through a positive feedback loop. In this mutual potentiation interaction, NIB1 uses both the IDR and the RNA-binding sites in the RRM to amplify and transduce NVR1-generated signalling molecules.

Right, reaction completion after 25 min, calculated as (intensity of hydrolysed RNA)/(intensity of undigested RNA) × 100%. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. b, Left, NIB1 (1 μM), but not NIB1(ΔIDR), stimulated NVR1 activity in a 25-min assay. Right, quantification of band intensity. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. c, 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p produced by NVR1 (1 μM) after co-incubation with NIB1 or NIB1(ΔIDR) (1 μM) for 25 min. d, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) (1 μM) activity in promoting the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p is compromised by NVR1 (1 μM), assayed for 25 min using rRNA as substrate (2 μg in 20 μl). In a–d, data are mean ± s.d. of n = 3 biologically independent replicates. Statistical differences were determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test.

NIB1 is highly expressed in multiple rice tissues (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To investigate the NIB1 function in plant defence, we used CRISPR–Cas9 to generate NIB1-knockout (NIB1-KO) and NIB1-overexpression (NIB1-OE) rice lines (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). NIB1-OE and NVR1-OE plants showed similar transcriptional changes, with 553 (59%) of the upregulated genes overlapping (Fig. 4b), including genes associated with response to biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence (Fig. 4c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 were downregulated in NIB1-KO plants but markedly upregulated in NIB1-OE plants (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the RNA-seq data and the levels of defence hormones salicylic acid and jasmonic acid (Fig. 4d). C. medinalis larvae gained more weight after feeding on the NIB1-KO lines than with the wild-type plants; by contrast, their growth was retarded on the NIB1-OE plants (Fig. 4e). Females and larvae preferred NIB1-KO over wild-type and NIB1-OE plants in oviposition and feeding-choice assays (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Insect feeding strongly induced MYC2 in wild-type rice, but the induction was much weaker in the NIB1-KO mutant (Fig. 4f). NIB1-OE plants had reduced tillering, partly resembling the NVR1-OE phenotype (Extended Data Fig. 2l), whereas NIB1-KO plants grew well and produced more tillers (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7h), probably reflecting their differences in immune intensity. These results suggest that NIB1 positively regulates plant defence responses.

Right, colour-coded stacked bars display the percentages of each cell death score (0–5; n = 11 leaves). i, Jasmonic acid and salicylic acid contents in ZH11, NIB1-KO and NIB1-KO leaves expressing NIB1, NIB1R49A or NIB1G50A in 12-day old rice plants. j, 2′,3′-cNMP binding mutations impaired NIB1-mediated resistance to insect feeding. Statistical differences were determined by two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test (g), one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s (d,e,i,j) or Dunnett’s (k) multiple-comparisons test.

We next investigated whether the NVR1-induced plant defence responses were contingent on the presence of NIB1. Treatment of rice plants with purified NVR1 induced ROS production, which was attenuated in NIB1-KO lines (Fig. 4g). Consistently, NVR1-induced cell death was mitigated in NbGRP7-KO leaves compared with wild-type N. benthamiana (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 7i,j). Thus, the RNA-binding protein NIB1 mediates NVR1-dependent induction of plant defence response.

To further determine whether NIB1 senses 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p to mediate NVR1-induced immune activation, we generated overexpression complementation lines in NIB1-KO rice plants, including wild-type NIB1, NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A. The two recognition-deficient complementation lines were unable to rescue the immune responses in NIB1-KO mutants, as indicated by defence hormone accumulation (Fig. 4i), insect resistance (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b) and the expression of MYC2, COI1 and NPR1 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Expression of NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A in wild-type rice plants did not lead to a clear upregulation of these defence genes (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Together, these results show that NIB1 activates plant defence against insect feeding and that sensing of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p is crucial for this immune function of NIB1.

MST assays with NIB1(ΔIDR) exhibited similar binding affinity to 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P as wild-type NIB1 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 8f). However, overexpression of NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP in NIB1-KO rice plants did not rescue the compromised insect resistance (Fig. 4k). Moreover, treatment with 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP induced condensate formation in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/NIB1-KO plants but not in 35S::NIB1ΔIDR-YFP/NIB1-KO plants (Extended Data Fig. 8g,h). Thus, both ligand recognition via RRM and subsequent phase separation via IDR are essential for the NIB1-dependent defence response.

To connect the NVR1–NIB1 module to the plant defence network, we performed IP–MS on leaves co-expressing NIB1–YFP and NVR1. EDS1, CDPK and MAPK6 were identified as NIB1 interactors (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Comparison with the NVR1 interactome revealed that the shared components were enriched in herbivore-response pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9b).

EDS1 is a central immune signalling node35,36,37. In SLC assays, NIB1 interacted with rice EDS1 (Extended Data Fig. 9c). EDS1–YFP co-immunoprecipitated with NIB1–Flag in N. benthamiana (Fig. 5a), and His–NIB1 pulled down EDS1–Flag from N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays showed that NIB1 interacted with EDS1 in the nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 9e), and the NIB1–EDS1 interaction was enhanced by NVR1 via its RNase activity (Fig. 5b). Catalytically active NVR1, but not the inactive NVR1(H-doub) mutant, stimulated NIB1 recruitment of EDS1 into sparkly nuclear condensates (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9f). We then used EDS1–NES–mCherry to test whether EDS1 acts as a nuclear carrier for NIB1. When EDS1–NES–mCherry was largely retained in the cytosol, NIB1 continued to form nuclear condensates in the presence of NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 9g), indicating that NIB1 nuclear condensation is independent of EDS1 and supporting the role of NIB1 as a scaffold for EDS1 recruitment.
